claims.sentence: The two terms are often mixed up, but the NHS and the British Heart Foundation (BHF) treat them as different emergencies.
claims.evidence: BHF page distinguishes heart attack (sudden loss of blood flow to part of the heart muscle) from cardiac arrest (heart suddenly stops pumping); both emergencies, call 999. 'Often mixed up' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The British Heart Foundation (BHF) explains that a heart attack and a cardiac arrest are different, and that both are emergencies.

claims.sentence: A heart attack happens when one of the coronary arteries becomes blocked.
claims.evidence: NHS: a heart attack happens when blood flow to the heart is blocked. 'Coronary arteries' not in retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: A heart attack happens when the blood flow to the heart is blocked.

claims.sentence: The heart muscle is cut off from its blood supply and can be damaged if the blockage is not treated.
claims.evidence: BHF: sudden loss of blood flow to part of the heart muscle. NHS: life-threatening and needs emergency treatment in hospital. Damage-if-untreated not stated in retrieved text.
claims.newSentence: The BHF describes a heart attack as a sudden loss of blood flow to part of the heart muscle, and the NHS says it can be life-threatening and needs emergency treatment in hospital.

claims.sentence: The person is usually conscious and breathing.
claims.evidence: Nothing retrieved states this; it could also falsely reassure.

claims.sentence: In a cardiac arrest the heart stops pumping effectively.
claims.evidence: BHF: cardiac arrest is when the heart suddenly stops pumping blood around the body.

claims.sentence: The person collapses, does not respond and is not breathing normally.
claims.evidence: Cardiac arrest: person quickly loses consciousness; NHS 111 Wales: not responding and not breathing (or breathing does not look normal).

claims.sentence: The BHF says a heart attack can sometimes lead to a cardiac arrest.
claims.evidence: BHF: a heart attack can lead to cardiac arrest, as a dangerous heart rhythm may develop.

claims.sentence: Angina is chest pain or discomfort that happens when the heart muscle does not get enough blood because the coronary arteries are partly narrowed.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: angina is chest pain caused when the heart's blood supply is temporarily restricted (BHF: reduced blood flow to the heart muscle). 'Partly narrowed coronary arteries' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Angina is chest pain or discomfort that happens when the blood supply to the heart muscle is temporarily reduced.

claims.sentence: It is a sign of coronary heart disease rather than a heart attack in itself.
claims.evidence: NHS CHD symptoms page title returned but no excerpt stating this. BHF: angina does not damage the heart muscle the way a heart attack does.
claims.newSentence: The BHF says the discomfort of angina does not damage the heart muscle in the way a heart attack does.

claims.sentence: The NHS says angina can feel like a mild, uncomfortable sensation, sometimes similar to indigestion.
claims.evidence: No retrieved text mentions indigestion or mild sensation.

claims.sentence: It is often brought on by physical activity or stress and usually passes with rest or a nitrate medicine.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: angina symptoms usually happen during exercise, pass within a few minutes, and can be relieved by rest or a nitrate tablet or spray. 'Stress' not retrieved. Attribution to a single page unconfirmed.
claims.newSentence: Angina symptoms usually happen during exercise and pass within a few minutes, and they can be eased by resting or by using a nitrate tablet or spray.

claims.sentence: Angina is not usually life-threatening, but the BHF notes that it can be a sign of a higher risk of a heart attack.
claims.evidence: Not in retrieved text; the first half could also reassure wrongly.

claims.sentence: The NHS lists chest pain that feels like pressure, heaviness, tightness or squeezing.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: chest pain that feels tight or squeezing (or crushing). 'Pressure' and 'heaviness' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS lists chest pain that feels tight or squeezing.

claims.sentence: The pain can spread to the arms, jaw, neck, back or tummy.
claims.evidence: NHS: pain can spread to arm, neck, jaw; NHS 111 Wales-type text: from the chest to arms, jaw, neck, back and tummy.

claims.sentence: Other signs include feeling sick, sweating, shortness of breath and light-headedness.
claims.evidence: NHS: shortness of breath, nausea, sweating (also pale or grey skin); light-headedness listed in the retrieved symptom text.

claims.sentence: Some people have few symptoms, and the NHS says this is more common in older people and people with diabetes.
claims.evidence: Retrieved text says only that symptoms can be milder than expected and women more often report back/jaw pain and breathlessness; nothing on older people or diabetes.

claims.sentence: A key difference from angina is that heart attack symptoms are not usually relieved by a nitrate tablet or spray.
claims.evidence: BHF: heart attack symptoms are similar to angina but more severe, last longer and are not relieved by rest or GTN spray.

claims.sentence: A person in cardiac arrest loses consciousness.
claims.evidence: Cardiac arrest usually happens suddenly, with the person quickly losing consciousness.

claims.sentence: They do not respond to touch or speech, and they are not breathing normally.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: not responding and not breathing (or breathing does not look normal). 'Touch or speech' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: They do not respond, and they are not breathing or their breathing does not look normal.

claims.sentence: Without treatment a cardiac arrest is usually fatal within minutes, according to the BHF, which is why speed matters.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: without treatment the person may die within minutes. 'Usually fatal' stronger than the text; attribution to BHF page not confirmed.
claims.newSentence: Without treatment a person in cardiac arrest may die within minutes, which is why speed matters.

claims.sentence: The NHS says to call 999 immediately if someone may be having a heart attack, even if the symptoms seem mild.
claims.evidence: NHS: call 999 for heart attack warning signs. 'Even if mild' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says to call 999 straight away if someone may be having a heart attack.

claims.sentence: If someone seems to be in cardiac arrest, the NHS advises calling 999 and starting CPR, with the call handler giving instructions.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: if someone is unresponsive and not breathing normally, call 999 and start CPR; the call taker will say where a defibrillator is. Attribution to NHS page unconfirmed (search blend).

claims.sentence: For angina, a GP appointment is the usual route for a first episode of chest pain.
claims.evidence: No retrieved support; steering a first episode of chest pain to a routine GP appointment lacks a 999 route. NHS: 999 for main warning signs, 111 for less severe symptoms such as racing or irregular heartbeat.
claims.newSentence: The NHS says to call 999 for the main warning signs of a heart attack, and to call NHS 111 for less severe symptoms such as a racing or irregular heartbeat.

claims.sentence: The BHF says that chest pain that comes on suddenly and does not stop after a few minutes of rest could be a heart attack, and that is a 999 situation.
claims.evidence: Retrieved BHF text says heart attack symptoms are not relieved by rest or GTN and call 999; the 'few minutes' cut-off is not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: The BHF says heart attack pain is not relieved by rest or a nitrate medicine, and that a heart attack is a 999 emergency.

claims.sentence: A heart attack is usually assessed with an ECG, which records the heart's electrical activity, and a blood test for troponin, a protein released when the heart muscle is damaged.
claims.evidence: Diagnosis page: ECG is the first test and records electrical activity; troponin blood test shows heart muscle damage.

claims.sentence: The site's pages on these tests give more detail.
claims.evidence: Meta pointer to other site pages; harmless.

claims.sentence: Treatment aims to restore blood flow to the heart muscle as quickly as possible.
claims.evidence: Retrieved: medicine or surgery may be needed to restore blood supply to the heart; emergency care is time-sensitive. 'As quickly as possible' not stated verbatim.
claims.newSentence: Treatment in hospital, with medicine or a procedure, aims to restore the blood supply to the heart.

claims.sentence: Angina is managed with medicines and changes that reduce the strain on the heart, and the care team decides the plan.
claims.evidence: Nothing retrieved on angina treatment.

claims.sentence: A heart attack happens when a coronary artery becomes blocked and the heart muscle loses its blood supply.
claims.evidence: As c02/c03: blood flow to the heart is blocked; 'coronary artery' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: A heart attack happens when the blood flow to the heart is blocked.

claims.sentence: In a cardiac arrest the heart stops pumping effectively, the person collapses and is not breathing normally.
claims.evidence: See c05, c06.

claims.sentence: Angina is chest pain from reduced blood flow to the heart and is a sign of coronary heart disease.
claims.evidence: Reduced blood flow supported; 'sign of coronary heart disease' not retrieved.
claims.newSentence: Angina is chest pain caused by a temporary reduction in the blood supply to the heart.

claims.sentence: Angina symptoms usually ease with rest or a nitrate medicine, whereas heart attack symptoms usually do not.
claims.evidence: Angina usually passes with rest or nitrate tablet/spray; heart attack symptoms not relieved by rest or GTN.

claims.sentence: For a suspected heart attack or cardiac arrest the NHS says to call 999 straight away.
claims.evidence: NHS: call 999 for heart attack signs; cardiac arrest: call 999 and start CPR.

claims.sentence: A heart attack is a blocked blood supply to the heart muscle, cardiac arrest is the heart stopping, and angina is chest pain that eases with rest.
claims.evidence: Heart attack: blood flow blocked; cardiac arrest: heart suddenly stops pumping; angina usually relieved by rest.

notes: Only 4 searches used; none returned page-level excerpts for the NHS cardiac arrest or angina pages, so several supported items rely on blended summaries (attribution to c11, c15, c22 URLs is not fully confirmed). Nothing retrieved on angina treatment, CHD link, older people/diabetes. Aspirin and GTN dosing text appeared in results but was deliberately not used.
